transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-05-15
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~60 minutes
Attendees: Carlos Mendez (Redwood AE), Priya Desai (Redwood SE), Jesse Park (BrightScale - Head of Infra), Maya Lin (BrightScale - ML Platform Lead), Omar Rahman (BrightScale - SRE)

Summary: quick technical deep dive on throughput tuning knobs — continuous batching, scheduler parameters, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache behavior, and quantization tradeoffs. Discussed hosted vs dedicated vs private/VPC considerations and asked BrightScale for traces for an experimental run.

Topics: throughput tuning, contiguous batching, scheduler knobs, max_num_seqs, token limits, KV cache, quantization (int8 vs fp16/32), VPC/on-prem deployment implications, security (KMS, audit logs, SOC2).

Transcript:
[00:00] Carlos Mendez: All right hey everyone thanks for joining, we wanted to spend this hour going through throughput tuning best practices and get a bit of a fingerprint of BrightScale's workload so we can recommend concrete knobs.
[00:18] Jesse Park: Yeah thanks Carlos, appreciate it. High level we want to push latency under 120ms p95 for short chat tokens while keeping cost reasonable. We're running 8xA100 in prod today and evaluating Dedicated vs hosted.
[00:32] Priya Desai: Great, quick clarifying q — when you say short chat tokens, what's your typical seq length distribution? Like majority 16-64 tokens or longer?
[00:40] Maya Lin: Most are short, yeah 12-48 tokens for user utterance, but we have a tail up to 512 for certain support transcripts. The tail is small but sensitive.
[00:54] Omar Rahman: Also want to highlight we have bursty traffic, multiple tenants, and we do have a hard token cap per request that we enforce in the app.
[01:08] Priya Desai: Perfect. So two things matter for throughput: batching policy and scheduler knobs (max_num_seqs, max_tokens_per_batch), and second the KV cache reuse for multi-turn. Continuous batching in Redwood — and this is the runtime bit — will aggregate requests into a rolling batch and service them as soon as there's either max_num_seqs or token-timeout.
[01:34] Jesse Park: Could you explain token-timeout? We had that in our prototype but weren't sure how it interacts with latency SLOs.
[01:40] Priya Desai: Sure — token-timeout (often called batch wait or latency target) is the max time the scheduler will wait to accumulate more sequences before firing the batch. If you set it too high you get high throughput but higher tail latency; too low and you underutilize the GPU. Typical starting point is 5-15ms for low-latency chat use cases.
[02:00] Carlos Mendez: Right, and combined with max_num_seqs you can shape batch composition. For example for BrightScale's short seqs we might use max_num_seqs=64 and token-timeout=10ms, and a max tokens per batch of ~16384 depending on model. That keeps p95 low and still gets batching efficiency.
[02:21] Maya Lin: What's the knob for max_num_seqs exactly? Is it number of concurrent sequences in the same batch?
[02:26] Priya Desai: Exactly — max_num_seqs is the upper bound on the number of sequences the scheduler will pack together. There's also a context of max tokens in total per batch; scheduler respects both.
[02:36] Jesse Park: How does the KV cache affect this? We saw weird memory pressure when many multi-turn sessions were cached.
[02:42] Priya Desai: Good question. KV cache (or past-key cache) stores activations for cached prefixes. Memory usage scales with number of cached sessions * sequence length * hidden size. Redwood supports eviction policies and optional prefix caching TTLs. For Dedicated private installs you can increase host memory and tweak cache TTL; or evict long-tail sessions to keep GPU memory stable.
[03:05] Omar Rahman: Are there runtime flags to prefer cache locality vs batch size? We want to avoid evicting useful prefixes during heavy bursts.
[03:12] Priya Desai: There are heuristics. You can pin high-value sessions (enterprise tiers) so they get preferential cached slots, and lower-value sessions are opportunistically cached. Also batch scheduling can be cache-aware: the scheduler tries to co-locate sequences that share prefixes to improve KV reuse, though that depends on arrival patterns.
[03:31] Jesse Park: Interesting — how does quantization play into throughput? We were experimenting with int8.
[03:36] Carlos Mendez: Quantization reduces memory bandwidth and compute for attention/ksoftmax paths. Int8 can give 2-3x throughput improvements in many cases, but accuracy regressions can appear on certain prompts. We recommend running an eval harness against your prompt sets. Priya, any notes?
[03:51] Priya Desai: Yeah, besides accuracy baseline, int8 changes memory layout and can alter kernel selection. In some runtimes it enables tensor cores better, reducing latency for large batches. But for very short requests, the conversion overhead and calibration can negate gains, so measure with your mix.
[04:10] Maya Lin: For our short-run low-latency users, if int8 hurts p95 we might prefer fp16 + better batching — do you see that trade-off commonly?
[04:18] Priya Desai: Absolutely, fp16 often has more predictable quality and for small sequence lengths the throughput gain of int8 is less. But for throughput-heavy backlogs int8 often wins.
[04:28] Jesse Park: Ok that makes sense. On Dedicated vs Hosted vs Private: security-wise we need KMS/HSM, audit logs retained 7 years, and SSO integration. How does that affect throughput or the knobs?
[04:42] Carlos Mendez: Functionally the knobs are the same. Private/VPC adds network and key access layers; encryption at rest/unsealing from HSM adds a small startup latency but doesn't change per-token performance. The main operational impact is you control memory/host sizing and can tune LRU cache eviction aggressively if you need to.
[05:00] Omar Rahman: For a Private on-prem deployment do you recommend more host RAM per GPU specifically for KV cache?
[05:07] Priya Desai: Yes, for large KV caches plan for host memory ~2-3x GPU memory depending on model and sequence lengths. Also ensure NVMe fast swap for large offload scenarios and monitor cache miss rates. We can provide guidance based on your traces.
[05:23] Jesse Park: Back to scheduler knobs — you mentioned max_tokens_per_batch. How do we pick that?
[05:29] Priya Desai: It's heuristic driven. Estimate average token length times target max_num_seqs, then set a cap so you don't overflow GPU memory. If you see OOMs, lower max_tokens_per_batch or increase seq pruning. Redwood runtime will also enforce hard caps to prevent OOMs.
[05:44] Maya Lin: Are there recommended defaults per model family? We're using a 30B-ish open model.
[05:50] Priya Desai: For 30B models, a safe starting point is max_num_seqs 32-64 with max_tokens_per_batch ~16-32k depending on hidden size. For 7B you can go much higher. We'll send a specific table in followup.
[06:05] Jesse Park: Can we run an experiment where Redwood runs our trace through the scheduler offline and simulates different knobs? That would be ideal before changing prod.
[06:13] Carlos Mendez: Yes, we can run offline replay against the scheduler and provide expected cost/latency tradeoffs. Action item: Jesse to share traces, Priya to run simulation.
[06:22] Omar Rahman: How granular are the metrics we can get? We want token-level cost and p50/p95/p99 histories.
[06:28] Carlos Mendez: Redwood Console gives token-level cost breakdown, per-route/model latency histograms, and KV cache hit/miss metrics. We can add custom traces for your tenant IDs.
[06:36] Maya Lin: We also wanted to know about autoscaling and burst capacity. If we throttle batching during bursts does Redwood provide fallback to smaller models to preserve latency?
[06:46] Priya Desai: Yes, smart routing can fallback to compatible cheaper variants or to dedicated reserved pool. You can configure automatic fallback rules that prioritize latency or cost.
[06:55] Jesse Park: Any common pitfalls you see in continuous batching configs?
[06:59] Priya Desai: A few: 1) setting token-timeout too long for chat yields bad tail latency; 2) not bounding max_tokens_per_batch leads to OOMs on long tails; 3) unmonitored KV cache growth; 4) assuming int8 will always help without running prompt-level evals.
[07:20] Carlos Mendez: Also for multi-tenant workloads be careful with fairness — packer heuristics might favor small short sequences that arrive first unless you enable tenant-aware quotas.
[07:31] Maya Lin: Good note. From BrightScale's side we'll prepare traces and a short eval set for quant checks.
[07:36] Jesse Park: Quick question on scheduler knobs exposure — are these runtime flags per deployment, or can we modify them per-model route in Console?
[07:44] Priya Desai: Both. In Hosted you can tune per-route settings via the Console and have experiment-level overrides. In Dedicated/Private you get runtime config files and also Console overlays if you use the Redwood control plane.
[07:58] Omar Rahman: If we do a Private on-prem, can we still use Redwood Console for observability?
[08:05] Carlos Mendez: Yes the control plane can be configured to integrate with your VPC and export metrics to your observability stack, or you can opt for the hosted Console with secure peering. We'll map options to your compliance needs.
[08:18] Maya Lin: Anything else we should be thinking about for throughput?
[08:21] Priya Desai: Monitor batch sizes over time, KV hit rates, tail token lengths, and CPU host-side bottlenecks. Sometimes the host input pipeline is the limiter, not GPU. Use async IO and prefetching.
[08:35] Jesse Park: Great. Let's recap next steps.
[08:38] Carlos Mendez: Recap: BrightScale to send traces + seq distribution, Redwood to run continuous batching sims and provide recommended knobs (max_num_seqs, token-timeout, max_tokens_per_batch), run a small int8 eval on your eval prompts, and follow-up call week of May 25th.
[08:52] Maya Lin: Sounds good.
[08:54] Omar Rahman: Thanks everyone.
[08:56] Carlos Mendez: Thanks, we'll send notes and the quant doc. Bye.

End of transcript.
